title: A Systematic Review of Crash Causes and Safety Trends in Automated Driving Systems and Advanced Driver Assistance Systems
content: As Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) and Automated Driving Systems (ADS) technologies become more prevalent, evaluating their safety performance in complex, real-world environments has emerged as a critical research priority. This study presents a systematic literature review of crashes involving vehicles equipped with ADAS and ADS. Using the PRISMA methodology, this review analyzed 51 peer-reviewed articles and books published between 2018 and 2025. Articles were identified through comprehensive searches of ScienceDirect, TRID, and the Transportation Research Record. The selected studies were organized into five thematic categories: safety and crash characteristics, human interaction and user behavior, testing tools and simulations, cybersecurity and perception risks, and policy and governance. Findings reveal that while AV technologies show promise in reducing crash severity and frequency, performance is highly context-dependent, affected by roadway geometry, weather, system limitations, and user behavior. ADAS-related crashes are more common on highways and often involve human error, whereas ADS crashes are more likely in urban settings and linked to system disengagements. The review also highlights significant gaps in data availability, standardized evaluation protocols, and human-machine interaction research. Despite growing literature, many studies rely heavily on simulations and legacy datasets, limiting generalizability. To support safer AV deployment, future research must prioritize real-world testing and user trust frameworks deployment strategies. This review offers a knowledge base to guide policymakers, researchers, and industry stakeholders in advancing the development and regulation of vehicle automation technologies.
